claims.claim: Root cause analysis is a structured method for analyzing serious adverse events, adapted from industrial accident investigation and now a standard error-analysis tool in health care.
The Joint Commission has mandated the use of RCA to analyze sentinel events since 1997.

A sentinel event is a patient safety event, not primarily related to the natural course of the patient's illness, that reaches the patient and results in death, permanent harm, or severe temporary harm; organizations are expected to complete a credible RCA and corrective action plan within roughly 45 business days of recognizing it.

RCA is a systems method that identifies latent (system) causes and active errors, keeping the focus on process conditions rather than assigning blame to individuals; RCA2 guidance directs teams to focus causal statements on system-level issues and excludes deliberately unsafe or criminal acts.
The 5 Whys technique repeatedly asks 'why?' until a root cause is reached and is attributed to Taiichi Ohno of the Toyota Production System; a problem may have multiple root causes.

The cause-and-effect (fishbone) diagram was introduced by Kaoru Ishikawa and groups possible causes into major categories commonly given as people, methods, equipment, materials, measurement, and environment.

The RCA2 action hierarchy ranks corrective actions by strength: stronger actions change the system (architectural/physical changes, forcing functions, simplification, standardization); intermediate actions include checklists, software prompts, read-backs, and reducing distractions; weaker actions rely on memory and vigilance (double checks, warnings/labels, new policy/memo, training/education). It recommends at least one strong or intermediate action per RCA, because weaker actions used alone rarely sustain improvement.

FMEA is a prospective, structured process used to identify system failures of high-risk processes before they occur, mapping each step, estimating likelihood, detectability, and impact, often combined into a risk-priority score; this makes it the proactive counterpart to reactive, retrospective RCA.
The process was renamed RCA2 (Root Cause Analyses and Actions) by the National Patient Safety Foundation to emphasize that a credible analysis must yield strong corrective actions.
An RCA distinguishes a direct cause, contributing causes, and the underlying root cause of an event.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether the 45-day RCA window is stated as calendar days or business days, and whether it is a strict mandate.
positions: StatPearls states organizations must complete the RCA within 45 business days of recognizing a sentinel event.
Various secondary summaries describe a ~45-day submission window and a 72-hour start expectation; The Joint Commission's own policy frames self-reporting and sharing as encouraged.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states 'roughly 45 business days' and frames the RCA and action plan as an accreditation expectation following a sentinel event, avoiding overly precise procedural claims and not reproducing Joint Commission standards text.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether RCA reliably produces effective, durable fixes.
positions: RCA is the expected response to serious events and, done well, yields system improvement.
The AHRQ PSNet primer notes studies find RCAs frequently rely on weak interventions and do not consistently produce sustainable solutions.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents RCA's intent and, honestly, the 'retrain and remind' failure mode, using the RCA2 action hierarchy to explain what a strong action looks like.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft contained only generic boilerplate ('a foundational concept', 'a simple way to apply it') with no substantive, sourced claims about RCA.

sourceRecords.title: Root Cause Analysis (Patient Safety Primer)
sourceRecords.provider: Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ), Patient Safety Network (PSNet)
sourceRecords.notes: Read via WebFetch this session. Supports: RCA as a structured method adapted from industrial accident investigation; the systems approach identifying active errors (human-system interface) and latent errors; 'The Joint Commission has mandated use of RCA to analyze sentinel events (such as wrong-site surgery) since 1997'; the critique that RCAs often rely on weak interventions and fail to produce sustainable solutions; and the RCA2 renaming to emphasize strong corrective actions. Synthesized in original prose.

sourceRecords.title: Medical Error Prevention and Root Cause Analysis
sourceRecords.notes: Read via WebFetch this session. Supports: the definition of a sentinel event (a safety event not primarily related to the natural course of the illness that reaches a patient and results in death, severe harm, or permanent harm); the Joint Commission expectation of a formal process for identifying sentinel events, conducting timely and credible RCAs, and implementing a corrective action plan; completion within 45 business days of recognizing a sentinel event; and RCA's retrospective, systems-over-blame orientation looking beyond individual mistakes. Facts only.

sourceRecords.title: Application of failure mode and effects analysis (FMEA) to improve medication safety in the dispensing process - a study at a teaching hospital, Sri Lanka
sourceRecords.notes: Open-access article read via WebFetch (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov canonical after redirect). Supports: 'FMEA is a prospective, team based, structured process used to identify system failures of high risk processes before they occur' and the use of Risk Priority Numbers (RPN = severity x frequency/occurrence x detection) to prioritize failure modes. Used to ground the RCA (reactive) versus FMEA (proactive) contrast. No substantial prose reproduced.
